title: Count Almost Equal Pairs I
statement:
Two positive integers are **almost equal** when at most one swap makes them equal, where a swap picks one of the two numbers and exchanges two of its digits (any two positions). A swap may bring zeros to the front; that is allowed, and they simply drop out of the value (swapping the digits of `30` gives `03`, which is `3`). Equal numbers need no swap, so they count as almost equal.

Every value in `nums` is a positive integer. Count the pairs of positions `i < j` whose values `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` are almost equal, and return that count.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct method checks every pair and tries every digit swap in both numbers. A tidier enumeration turns the question around: one number can become only a handful of values with a single swap (at most 21 swaps of 7 digits, plus itself), so list those values and look up how many earlier numbers equal one of them.

One detail lets us look in a single direction. A swap never adds digits, so when two numbers have different lengths, only the longer one can turn into the shorter one (the zero it moves to the front drops out). When the lengths are equal, a swap works in one number exactly when the same swap works in the other. Sorting `nums` ascending therefore makes the current number the one worth swapping.

## Approach

1. Sort `nums` ascending.
2. For each `num`, start `reachable` with `num` itself, then for every pair of positions `i < j` swap them in `digits`, record the value, and swap back.
3. For every value in `reachable`, add how many earlier numbers had that value (`seen`).
4. Count `num` in `seen` for the numbers after it.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted, `nums = [3, 12, 17, 21, 30]`.

- `3` reaches `{3}`, `12` reaches `{12, 21}` and `17` reaches `{17, 71}`; nothing earlier matches.
- `21` reaches `{21, 12}`; `12` was seen once, so `pairs = 1`.
- `30` reaches `{30, 3}`; `3` was seen once, so `pairs = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n + n · d³) with d ≤ 7 digits: sorting, then d(d − 1)/2 swaps per number, each joining d digits.
- Space: O(n + d²) for `seen` and `reachable`.

## Pitfalls

- Swapping only inside `nums[i]` for each pair misses `3` and `30`: the longer number must be the one that changes.
- Compare values, not digit strings: `"03"` has to match `3`.
- Keep `reachable` a set: swapping two equal digits gives `num` again and would count the same earlier numbers twice.
- Equal numbers are almost equal with zero swaps.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `seen` | how many processed numbers have each value |
| `pairs` | almost equal pairs found so far |
| `num` | the current number |
| `digits` | its digits as characters, swapped in place |
| `reachable` | the values `num` can become with at most one swap |
| `i`, `j` | the two positions being swapped |
| `value` | one reachable value being looked up |
